sections.heading: A web ACL checks each HTTP request against its rules in priority order

plan.problem: Good requests and harmful requests arrive in the same stream. Something must read each request and decide before the application does. Term at first use: **web ACL** (web access control list), with a needs-term marker until the term is in the bank; say once that the console now calls it a protection pack (see Changed recently considered list: no entry, one clause only).
trace: Forward: the associated resources [forward incoming requests to AWS WAF] (waf-associated-resources-forward-requests).

Evaluate in order: AWS WAF evaluates rules [from the lowest numeric priority setting on up] (waf-rules-evaluated-lowest-priority-first); each rule has [a unique priority setting] (waf-rule-priority-unique).

Match: a rule statement reads one part of the request. In one sentence or a short list: an SQL injection statement [inspects for malicious SQL code] (waf-sqli-statement-inspects-malicious-sql); an XSS statement [inspects for malicious scripts] (waf-xss-statement-inspects-malicious-scripts); an IP set is a [collection of IP addresses and IP address ranges] (waf-ip-set-collection-of-addresses); a geo match works [based on country and region of origin] (waf-geo-match-country-and-region); a managed rule group adds [collections of predefined, ready-to-use rules] (waf-managed-rule-groups-definition).

Act: Allow and Block are terminating: a terminating action [stops the protection pack (web ACL) evaluation] (waf-terminating-vs-non-terminating). Count is not: [AWS WAF continues processing the remaining rules] (waf-count-non-terminating-continues).

Default: a request that passes every rule [without having a terminating action applied to it] gets the default action, Allow or Block (waf-default-action-required-applies-no-terminating, waf-default-action-allow-or-block).
plan.table: Truth table 'What happens to the request' (columns: The rule result | Evaluation | The request). Allow matches | stops | goes to the resource. Block matches | stops | is blocked; [you can customize the response] (waf-block-default-403). Count matches | continues | meets the next rule. No rule ends it | ends at the default action | Allow or Block. Four rows.
plan.why: Why a default action? Every request needs a final answer. To allow most traffic and stop only some, set the [default action to Allow] and add rules that block (waf-default-allow-add-block-rules).
plan.exam_signal: "block SQL injection with the LEAST operational overhead" points to an AWS managed rule group, such as the SQL database group, which blocks patterns [like SQL injection attacks] (waf-sql-database-group); AWS and Marketplace sellers [automatically update managed rule groups] (waf-managed-rules-auto-updated).
plan.exam_trap: edge-protection-trap-nacl-for-many-attack-ips: the Exam trap callout, at most 60 words, ends with <!-- trap: edge-protection-trap-nacl-for-many-attack-ips -->. Truth with links: [20 rules per network ACL] by default (vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl); one AWS WAF IP set holds [10,000] addresses or ranges (waf-ip-set-max-addresses).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for edge-protection-t01 after the Exam trap, ending with <!-- task: edge-protection-t01 -->.
plan.spot_the_bug: The one Spot the bug of the file. '**Spot the bug.** A web ACL has two rules. Priority 0 allows every request whose URI path starts with /api. Priority 1 is the AWS managed core rule set, with its rules in Block. The default action is Allow. What is wrong?' Reveal: requests to /api never meet the core rule set, because Allow is terminating (waf-terminating-vs-non-terminating) and rules run [from the lowest numeric priority setting on up] (waf-rules-evaluated-lowest-priority-first). Fix: give the managed rule group the lower priority number, or narrow the Allow rule.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: rules run in priority order, and the first Allow or Block decides. The thing to watch is an early Allow rule.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A web ACL has the default action Block and one rule: Count requests that come from a partner's IP set. A partner sends a normal request. What happens to the request?' Answer: it is blocked. Count is non-terminating (waf-count-non-terminating-continues), so the request reaches the default action (waf-default-action-required-applies-no-terminating), which is Block.

sections.heading: Each resource has one web ACL in the same Region as the resource

plan.problem: A web ACL protects only the resource it is attached to. You choose the resource that receives the HTTP requests, and you create the web ACL in the right Region.
trace: Choose the resource: a web ACL can protect [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer], [AWS AppSync, Amazon Cognito, AWS App Runner] and a few more; for API Gateway the protected type is the [Amazon API Gateway REST API] (waf-protected-resource-types). A Network Load Balancer and an EC2 instance are not on that list; do not write 'cannot' for them (no saved page says it): write that the list does not name them, with the link.

Create it in the right Region: the web ACL and the resources it uses must be in [the Region where the associated resource is located]; for CloudFront that is [US East (N. Virginia)] (waf-web-acl-region-of-resource). An IP set for CloudFront too: [you must use Global (CloudFront)] (waf-ip-set-global-for-cloudfront).

Associate: each resource takes [with only one protection pack (web ACL)], and one web ACL can serve many resources: [one-to-many] (waf-one-web-acl-per-resource). A web ACL on CloudFront cannot be associated [with any other AWS resource type] (waf-cloudfront-web-acl-not-other-types).

Run: on CloudFront [your rules run in all AWS Edge Locations], and blocked requests are [stopped before they reach your web servers] (waf-cloudfront-rules-run-at-edge). On a regional resource the rules run in its Region and protect [internet-facing resources as well as internal resources] (waf-regional-rules-run-in-region-internal).
plan.table: Columns: Resource | Create the web ACL in | Where the rules run. Rows: CloudFront distribution | US East (N. Virginia), shown as Global (CloudFront) | edge locations. ALB, API Gateway REST API, AppSync, Cognito | the resource's own Region | that Region. A website outside AWS | put CloudFront in front: it [supports custom origins outside of AWS] (waf-protect-sites-outside-aws-via-cloudfront) | edge locations. Three rows.
plan.why: Why one Region for CloudFront? A distribution serves from edge locations everywhere, so its web ACL needs one home: the console choice Global (CloudFront) is [identical to choosing Region US East (N. Virginia)] (waf-global-cloudfront-equals-us-east-1).
plan.exam_signal: "protect a website that runs in the company's own data center from SQL injection" points to a CloudFront distribution with a web ACL, because CloudFront [supports custom origins outside of AWS] (waf-protect-sites-outside-aws-via-cloudfront).
plan.exam_trap: none in this subsection (the trap edge-protection-trap-waf-on-any-resource is in the fast traps list; the brief trap cap leaves no callout here). The body sentence on the NLB carries the point.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: large request bodies (at most 90 words). For an ALB and AWS AppSync, AWS WAF inspects a body of [8 KB] (waf-body-limit-alb-appsync-8kb); for CloudFront, API Gateway, Cognito, App Runner and Verified Access the limit is [16 KB] by default and can be raised to [64 KB] (waf-body-limit-default-16kb-max-64kb). The host [forwards the contents that are within the limit] (waf-body-forwarded-only-within-limit), and the oversize option of a rule decides: Continue, Match or No match (waf-oversize-handling-options); [Outside the console, the default option is Continue.] (waf-oversize-default-continue).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: attach the web ACL to the resource that receives the requests. The thing to watch is the Region for CloudFront.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team wants AWS WAF on a CloudFront distribution and on an Application Load Balancer in Europe (Ireland). How many web ACLs does it need, and where does it create them?' Answer: two. One in US East (N. Virginia) for the distribution (waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1), because a CloudFront web ACL cannot be associated [with any other AWS resource type] (waf-cloudfront-web-acl-not-other-types); one in Europe (Ireland) for the load balancer (waf-web-acl-region-of-resource).

sections.heading: A rate-based rule limits each key that sends requests too fast

plan.problem: A sign-in page can be flooded by automated requests. A list of attacking addresses must be edited by hand; a rule that reacts to how fast each source sends needs no list. Term at first use: **rate-based rule** (needs-term marker until it is in the bank).
trace: Group: the rule aggregates requests by a key, by default [based on the request IP address] (waf-rate-based-default-key-ip); you can choose [various other aggregation keys and key combinations].
Count: it counts each group over its evaluation window, [5 minutes] by default, from [1 minute] to [10 minutes] (waf-rate-window-options).

Compare: each group is compared with the request limit; the lowest limit is [10] (waf-rate-limit-minimum). The rule counts and limits [evaluation window, request limit, and action settings] per group (waf-rate-based-counts-and-limits).
Act: an address over the limit is blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold] (waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls).

Scope down: to protect one page, use [a rate-based rule with a scope-down statement] (waf-rate-based-scope-down). With the Count all option every matching request counts together, and [This option requires a scope-down statement.] (waf-rate-based-count-all-needs-scope-down).
plan.table: Truth table 'Which rule stops which sign-in attack' (columns: Attack | Rate-based rule per IP address | Count all on the sign-in page | ATP managed rule group). Row 1: a few addresses, many requests each | blocks those addresses | limits every user of the page | checks the passwords. Row 2: many addresses, few requests each | no address passes the limit | limits every user of the page | checks each sign-in [against its stolen credential database] (waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts). Two rows. The ATP group is paid: the Bot Control, ATP and ACFP groups [are available for additional fees] (waf-managed-paid-groups-bot-atp-acfp).
plan.why: Why count per key? One noisy source is limited and other users keep working. AWS designed rate-based rules for [brute force login attempts] and [web-layer DDoS attacks] (waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos).
plan.exam_signal: "one IP address sends too many requests" or "brute force login attempts" points to a rate-based rule (waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos); "stolen" or [compromised credentials] (waf-faq-atp-login-page) points to the ATP managed rule group.
plan.exam_trap: edge-protection-trap-per-ip-rate-limit-stops-all: one new case beyond the table, at most 60 words, for example a bank's supervisors who all sign in from one office address and hit a per-IP limit together; the truth links waf-rate-based-default-key-ip. End with <!-- trap: edge-protection-trap-per-ip-rate-limit-stops-all -->.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: a rate limit is not exact (at most 90 words). Rate limiting [does not guarantee an exact limit match] (waf-rate-based-not-precise); detection can lag [for up to several minutes], and usually [this delay is below 30 seconds] (waf-rate-based-detection-delay). Behind CloudFront, a web ACL on the load balancer sees [the address of the last proxy] (waf-forwarded-ip-default-origin-ip); a rule can [use a forwarded IP address] instead (waf-forwarded-ip-statements), but [Attackers might alter the contents of the header] (waf-forwarded-header-can-be-spoofed). Before Block, run new rules in Count: AWS advises to [test and tune your rules in count mode] (waf-test-in-count-mode-before-production).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: count requests per address and block the ones that go too fast. The thing to watch is many slow addresses.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A sign-in page receives about four attempts from each of 1,400 IP addresses in every five-minute window. A rate-based rule limits each IP address to 100 requests in five minutes. Does the rule block the attack?' Answer: no. The rule counts each address separately (waf-rate-based-counts-and-limits), and every address stays under its limit. Add the ATP managed rule group, which checks sign-ins [against its stolen credential database] (waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts). Do not put a new number with a unit in the reveal.

sections.heading: Shield Standard protects every account free but Shield Advanced adds paid response

plan.problem: A DDoS attack tries to make an application unavailable. Some attacks flood the network with packets; others send web requests that look normal. Term: **DDoS attack** (distributed denial of service), needs-term marker until it is in the bank.
trace: Always on: Shield Standard protects [for all AWS customers] against [layer 3 and 4] events such as SYN floods and UDP reflection (shield-faq-standard-layer-3-4-all-customers), [at no additional charge] (shield-standard-automatic-no-charge); its [protection is automatic and non-configurable] (shield-standard-non-configurable).

Web floods need AWS WAF: Shield [does not inspect the contents] of HTTP traffic (shield-no-http-content-inspection); against [HTTP POST or GET floods] you use AWS WAF (shield-faq-standard-use-waf-for-layer-7).

Subscribe: Shield Advanced [provides expanded DDoS attack protection] (shield-advanced-paid-expanded-protection), for resources [explicitly specified in Shield Advanced] (shield-advanced-not-automatic-per-resource).

Get help and credits: Shield Advanced adds [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team] (shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection), with the [Business Support plan] or Enterprise Support (shield-srt-needs-business-or-enterprise-support), and you can [request a Shield Advanced service credit] for charges caused by an attack (shield-cost-protection-credit).
plan.table: Truth table 'Who stops which attack' (columns: Attack | Shield Standard alone | Shield Standard and AWS WAF | Shield Advanced). Row 1: SYN flood | mitigated | mitigated | mitigated, with the response team. Row 2: HTTP GET flood | not inspected | a rate-based rule | AWS WAF, with the response team. Row 3: scaling charges caused by the attack | you pay | you pay | service credit. Link one fact per strict claim cell; keep cells at most 15 words. Do not repeat the fast compare table (cost, resources, experts): this table is about attacks.
plan.why: Why pay for Advanced? It buys people and predictable costs: AWS suggests it for [Rapid access to DDoS mitigation experts] and [Predictability in your cloud costs] (shield-advanced-when-to-subscribe).
plan.exam_signal: "24/7 access to the AWS DDoS response team" or "protection against charges caused by a DDoS attack" points to Shield Advanced (shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection, shield-cost-protection-credit).
plan.exam_trap: edge-protection-trap-network-firewall-stops-ddos: at most 60 words; truth links [but not to mitigate volumetric attacks] (network-firewall-not-for-ddos). End with <!-- trap: edge-protection-trap-network-firewall-stops-ddos -->.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Shield Standard is already on, and Shield Advanced adds experts and cost credits. The thing to watch is the yearly commitment.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A company subscribes to Shield Advanced on Monday. On Tuesday its Application Load Balancer is attacked and scales out. During the attack, an engineer adds the load balancer as a protected resource. Can the company get a credit for the scaling charges?' Answer: no. Resources [added during an attack are not eligible] (shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack); add protection before an attack.

sections.heading: Network Firewall inspects VPC traffic only when route tables send it there

plan.problem: A security group or a network ACL filters by address and port: they give [traffic control at a Layer 4 level (IP address and port ranges)] (well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services). A rule such as 'only these software update domains' needs a firewall that reads names in the traffic. Term at first use: **firewall endpoint** (needs-term marker). Use **egress** (EE-gress) once for outbound traffic (bank term).
trace: Place: firewall endpoints are installed [on a per-Availability Zone basis] (network-firewall-endpoints-per-az), each in a dedicated subnet of [a minimum size of /28] (network-firewall-faq-dedicated-subnet-28), reserved [for the exclusive use of Network Firewall] (network-firewall-endpoint-not-own-subnet).

Route: [you modify your Amazon VPC route tables] (network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection); the firewall inspects [all traffic that is routed to the endpoint] (network-firewall-faq-inspects-routed-traffic).

Stateless engine first: the packet meets [the policy's stateless rule groups first] (network-firewall-stateless-then-stateful); each packet alone, like [Amazon VPC network access control lists (ACLs)] (network-firewall-stateless-like-nacl); pass, drop, or forward to stateful (network-firewall-stateless-actions).

Stateful engine: a domain list reads the [Server Name Indication (SNI) extension] of HTTPS and the HTTP host header (network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header); an allow list denies other domains [when the firewall policy uses default action order] (network-firewall-domain-allow-denies-others).

Return: the reply comes back through [the Network Firewall endpoint in both directions] (network-firewall-no-asymmetric-routing), then the NAT gateway and the internet gateway carry the allowed traffic.
plan.table: Columns: Engine | Looks at | Works like | Actions. Stateless | each packet alone | a network ACL (network-firewall-stateless-like-nacl) | pass, drop, forward (network-firewall-stateless-actions). Stateful | the whole flow, domain names, payload | a security group, but by default [the stateful rules engine allows traffic to pass] (network-firewall-stateful-like-sg-default-pass) | pass, drop, reject, alert (network-firewall-stateful-actions). Two rows.
plan.why: Why routes? The firewall is one hop on the path: it inspects [all traffic that is routed to the endpoint] (network-firewall-faq-inspects-routed-traffic), so the route tables decide which paths are inspected.
plan.exam_signal: "filter outbound traffic by domain name" or "intrusion prevention for traffic in the VPC" points to Network Firewall, a managed [intrusion detection and prevention service] (network-firewall-definition).
plan.exam_trap: edge-protection-trap-sg-filters-domains: at most 60 words, a new case (for example an outbound security group rule that names a software update site); truth links [You can specify allow rules, but not deny rules] (vpc-sg-allow-rules-only) or well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services, and network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists. End with <!-- trap: edge-protection-trap-sg-filters-domains -->.
plan.try_it: Try it callout for edge-protection-t02 (optional task) after the Exam trap, ending with <!-- task: edge-protection-t02 -->. If edge-protection-t02 is not written, leave the callout out.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: encrypted traffic, rule order and many VPCs (at most 90 words). A domain list reads names without decryption; to inspect the content, TLS inspection configurations [decrypt your firewall's inbound and outbound SSL/TLS traffic] and re-encrypt it (network-firewall-tls-inspection-decrypt-reencrypt), with certificates in AWS Certificate Manager (network-firewall-tls-needs-acm-new-policy). Under strict order the allow list denies nothing else, so choose Drop established, the option [for your own domain list rule groups] (network-firewall-strict-default-actions). For many VPCs, one firewall can attach to a transit gateway through [the native integration capability] or sit in an inspection VPC (network-firewall-faq-tgw-native-or-manual).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: route the traffic through a firewall endpoint with a domain list. The thing to watch is the return path.
plan.stop_and_answer: 'A team puts the firewall endpoint in the same subnet as the application instances that it must protect. Does the firewall inspect the traffic of those instances?' Answer: no. An endpoint protects the other subnets of the VPC, not its own; firewall subnets are [for the exclusive use of Network Firewall] (network-firewall-endpoint-not-own-subnet). Do not link the display that holds a contraction.

sections.heading: Firewall Manager applies the same protections to every account in an organization

plan.problem: An organization adds accounts every month. Rules that each team copies by hand drift apart, and a new account starts with no rules.
trace: Prepare: Firewall Manager has [three mandatory pre-requisites and one optional pre-requisite] (firewall-manager-prereqs-faq-list): an organization with all features (firewall-manager-needs-org-all-features), [the Firewall Manager administrator account] (firewall-manager-faq-prereq-administrator-account), and AWS Config in each account and Region: [you must enable AWS Config] (firewall-manager-requires-aws-config).

Write a policy: each policy is [specific to the individual policy type] (firewall-manager-policy-types), and [security policies are region specific] (firewall-manager-policies-region-specific); for CloudFront you choose Global (firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront).

Scope it: all accounts, a list of included accounts and OUs, or all except a list (firewall-manager-scope-accounts-ous), or resource tags (firewall-manager-scope-resource-tags). Spell out OU (organizational unit) at first use.

Apply it: report only, which [does not enforce the rules on the resources] (firewall-manager-manual-remediation-mode), or [automatically remediate noncompliant resources] (firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate); in a new account [Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy] (firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts). Findings go to AWS Security Hub (firewall-manager-findings-to-security-hub).
plan.table: Columns: Policy type | What it puts in each account. AWS WAF | a web ACL with [rule groups to run first and last] (firewall-manager-waf-policy-first-last-rule-groups). Security group | [common security groups to specified accounts and resources], and audits (firewall-manager-sg-policy-three-uses). Network Firewall | firewalls and endpoints, distributed or centralized (firewall-manager-nfw-policy-management-models). Three rows.
plan.why: Why first and last rule groups? The security team keeps the rules that must run in every account, and each owner adds [rules and rule groups to run in between] (firewall-manager-waf-policy-first-last-rule-groups).

sections.plan: Exactly 5 FAQ items (see faq), each a can-or-cannot question, the short answer with its fact link, then one AWS quote block of whole sentences of the fact's evidence quote, attributed to its FAQ page. At most 240 words.

traps.belief: AWS WAF can protect any resource that receives traffic, such as a Network Load Balancer or an EC2 instance.
traps.truth: A web ACL protects the resource types that AWS WAF lists, such as CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer and an API Gateway REST API; that list does not name a Network Load Balancer, which Shield Advanced protects through its Elastic IP addresses.

traps.belief: AWS Shield blocks harmful content in web requests, and AWS WAF stops floods of network packets.
traps.truth: Shield inspects at the packet level and does not inspect the contents of HTTP traffic; AWS WAF inspects at the request level and protects against exploits such as SQL injection.

traps.belief: Without a Shield Advanced subscription, an application on AWS has no DDoS protection.
traps.truth: Shield Standard protects all AWS customers automatically, at no additional charge, against common network and transport layer attacks; Shield Advanced is a paid subscription that adds expanded protection.

traps.belief: A network ACL deny list is the right tool to block an attack that comes from many IP addresses.
traps.truth: A network ACL has 20 rules by default; an AWS WAF IP set holds up to 10,000 addresses or ranges, and a rate-based rule blocks each address only while its request rate stays too high.

traps.belief: A rate-based rule that limits each IP address stops every automated sign-in attack.
traps.truth: A rate-based rule counts and limits each aggregation key separately, by default the IP address, so an attack spread over many addresses can stay under the limit; a scope-down rule with Count all or the ATP managed rule group handles that case.

traps.belief: AWS Network Firewall protects a VPC against volumetric DDoS attacks.
traps.truth: Network Firewall controls access to and from a VPC but is not designed to mitigate volumetric attacks; AWS recommends the DDoS resiliency best practices and AWS Shield Advanced.

traps.belief: Security group rules can limit outbound traffic to approved domain names.
traps.truth: Security groups and route tables control traffic at layer 4, by IP address and port range; Network Firewall stateful domain lists read the domain name in the traffic.

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair 1 (twin q05)
question_slots.note: Shared scenario: 'A company runs an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances reach the internet through NAT gateways.' Changed phrase of q01: 'Attackers send requests that contain SQL injection code to the application.' Ask: 'Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical in q05, in neutral words: (A) Associate a web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer. (B) Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and send the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints. (C) Add security group and network ACL rules that match the approved domain names and the content of the requests. (D) Run a fleet of proxy servers on EC2 instances that inspect every inbound request and every outbound connection. Key of q01: A (waf-sql-database-group, waf-managed-rules-auto-updated). Wrong: B different-problem (misconception: a domain list rule group reads the content of requests to a load balancer); C impossible-feature, trap edge-protection-trap-sg-filters-domains (well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services); D violates-qualifier (misconception: a self-managed proxy fleet is the simplest control).

A web application on EC2 instances serves HTTP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. The security team must block common web exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Key: replace the Network Load Balancer with an Application Load Balancer and associate a web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with it (waf-protected-resource-types, waf-core-rule-set-owasp). Wrong: associate the web ACL with the Network Load Balancer (wrong-configuration, trap edge-protection-trap-waf-on-any-resource; type it impossible-feature only if the open-book solver accepts waf-protected-resource-types as proof); subscribe to Shield Advanced and protect the load balancer's Elastic IP addresses (sibling-confusion, trap edge-protection-trap-shield-and-waf-swapped; shield-no-http-content-inspection); install an open source web firewall on each instance and update its rules every week (violates-qualifier).

A login page behind CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer receives thousands of requests each minute from a small set of IP addresses that changes every few hours; real users send few requests. Key: add a rate-based rule that blocks IP addresses above a request limit to a web ACL on the CloudFront distribution (waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls, waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos). Wrong: network ACL deny rules for the addresses, updated when they change (wrong-configuration, trap edge-protection-trap-nacl-for-many-attack-ips); subscribe to Shield Advanced and ask the response team to block them (violates-qualifier, trap edge-protection-trap-ddos-needs-shield-advanced; why links shield-advanced-one-year-commitment, never the price); inbound deny rules in the load balancer's security group (impossible-feature, trap vpc-trap-sg-deny; vpc-sg-allow-rules-only). No number from the canon decides the key.

question_slots.worked: think-aloud, wrong_path false (the chapter's one worked question)
question_slots.note: A web ACL on a CloudFront distribution has a rate-based rule per IP address. Attackers now try stolen user names and passwords against the sign-in page from thousands of IP addresses; each address sends a few requests an hour, below the limit. Real users must keep signing in during the attack. Key: add the AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention (ATP) managed rule group to the web ACL for the sign-in page (waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts, waf-faq-atp-login-page). Wrong: lower the request limit of the per-IP rule (wrong-configuration, trap edge-protection-trap-per-ip-rate-limit-stops-all; do not name the minimum value, it changed in 2024); a scope-down rate-based rule with Count all that blocks all sign-in requests above a limit (wrong-configuration: it also blocks real users; waf-rate-based-scope-down, waf-rate-based-count-all-needs-scope-down; the second finalist); an IP set built each day from the logs (violates-qualifier, misconception: a daily block list keeps up with the attack). The stem says the sign-in page is served through CloudFront, not an Amazon Cognito user pool (waf-cognito-no-atp-acfp).

The instances must reach only an approved list of software update domains.' Key: B (network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists, network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header, network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection). Wrong: A sibling-confusion (misconception: a web ACL on the load balancer filters the instances' outbound traffic); C impossible-feature, trap edge-protection-trap-sg-filters-domains; D violates-qualifier. The twin line of each quotes the other's changed phrase.

Qualifier none (difficulty 1). A small company serves its website through Amazon CloudFront and is worried about SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks; it has never subscribed to any AWS Shield plan. Which service already protects the website against these attacks? Key: AWS Shield Standard, which protects every AWS customer automatically at no additional charge (shield-standard-automatic-no-charge, shield-faq-standard-layer-3-4-all-customers). Wrong: nothing until the company subscribes to Shield Advanced (sibling-confusion, trap edge-protection-trap-ddos-needs-shield-advanced); AWS WAF, after a web ACL with a rate-based rule is associated (sibling-confusion, trap edge-protection-trap-shield-and-waf-swapped); AWS Network Firewall in the origin's VPC (different-problem, trap edge-protection-trap-network-firewall-stops-ddos). No violates-qualifier option.

A mission-critical application runs behind CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer; the company has an Enterprise Support plan. During DDoS attacks it must get help from AWS DDoS experts at any hour and must be able to recover scaling charges that an attack causes. Key: subscribe to Shield Advanced now and add the distribution and the load balancer as protected resources, each with a web ACL that has a rate-based rule in Block mode (shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection, shield-cost-protection-credit, shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack). Wrong: rely on Shield Standard and open a support case during an attack (misconception: Shield Standard includes the response team and credits); subscribe to Shield Advanced but add the resources when an attack starts (wrong-configuration; shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack); route inbound traffic through Network Firewall and request refunds from AWS Billing (violates-qualifier and different-problem, trap edge-protection-trap-network-firewall-stops-ddos).

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features and adds accounts every month. The security team must make sure that the same AWS WAF rules protect every Application Load Balancer and CloudFront distribution, also in new accounts. Key: enable AWS Config, set a Firewall Manager administrator account, and create Firewall Manager AWS WAF policies: one with the Global choice for CloudFront and one for each Region that runs load balancers (firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts, firewall-manager-requires-aws-config, firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront). Wrong: a daily script that creates and associates a web ACL in each account (violates-qualifier); turn on Firewall Manager in each account without an administrator account and write one policy for all Regions (impossible-feature, misconception that Firewall Manager needs no organization setup; firewall-manager-faq-prereq-administrator-account, firewall-manager-policies-region-specific); subscribe the organization to Shield Advanced so that AWS applies web exploit rules everywhere (sibling-confusion, trap edge-protection-trap-shield-and-waf-swapped).

Qualifier none. A developer creates a web ACL and an IP set in Europe (Ireland) to protect a CloudFront distribution; the distribution does not appear in the list of resources to associate. What should the developer do? Key: create the web ACL and the IP set again in US East (N. Virginia), the Global (CloudFront) choice, and associate the web ACL with the distribution (waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1, waf-ip-set-global-for-cloudfront). Wrong: associate the IP set directly with the distribution (wrong-configuration; waf-ip-set-collection-of-addresses: a rule statement references the set); create the web ACL in the Region of the distribution's origin (wrong-configuration, misconception: a CloudFront web ACL follows the origin's Region); enable Shield Advanced on the distribution first (keyword-bait, trap edge-protection-trap-shield-and-waf-swapped).

A VPC has public and private subnets in three Availability Zones and a NAT gateway in each zone. All traffic between the internet and the private workloads must be inspected by AWS Network Firewall, and the design must keep working when one zone fails, MOST resilient. Keys: a dedicated firewall subnet with a firewall endpoint in each Availability Zone (network-firewall-endpoints-per-az, network-firewall-subnet-per-az-required, network-firewall-faq-dedicated-subnet-28); route each zone's traffic in both directions through the endpoint in the same zone (network-firewall-no-asymmetric-routing, network-firewall-two-az-same-zone-routing). Wrong: one endpoint in one zone for all three zones (violates-qualifier, misconception: one endpoint can serve every zone); the endpoints in the same subnets as the workloads (impossible-feature; network-firewall-endpoint-not-own-subnet); a web ACL on the internet gateway (sibling-confusion, trap edge-protection-trap-waf-on-any-resource).

A website runs behind CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer. An HTTP GET flood from many IP addresses slows it down. The company has only Shield Standard and wants protection against such floods, MOST cost-effective, with no long-term commitment. Keys: associate a web ACL with the distribution and add a rate-based rule that blocks IP addresses above a limit (waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos, waf-cloudfront-rules-run-at-edge); add the Amazon IP reputation list managed rule group to the same web ACL (waf-ip-reputation-list-group; basic pricing applies: waf-managed-rule-groups-definition, not one of the paid groups of waf-managed-paid-groups-bot-atp-acfp). Wrong: subscribe to Shield Advanced (violates-qualifier, trap edge-protection-trap-ddos-needs-shield-advanced; why links shield-advanced-one-year-commitment, not the price); network ACL deny rules for the addresses (wrong-configuration, trap edge-protection-trap-nacl-for-many-attack-ips); Network Firewall stateful rules for inbound traffic (different-problem, trap edge-protection-trap-network-firewall-stops-ddos). Do not use the Anti-DDoS managed rule group as a key: it is new (2025-06) and charged extra.

A company with many accounts in AWS Organizations finds security groups that allow SSH from any address. The security team must find such rules in every account and fix them automatically, also in new accounts, with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: a Firewall Manager content audit security group policy with automatic remediation for all accounts (firewall-manager-sg-policy-three-uses, firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate, firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts). Wrong: an AWS WAF web ACL with a rule that blocks port 22 on each instance (impossible-feature, trap edge-protection-trap-waf-on-any-resource; waf-protected-resource-types); a Network Firewall stateless rule in each VPC that drops port 22 (different-problem: the open rules stay; misconception); a monthly manual review by each account owner (violates-qualifier). The stem may state the port and the open range as scenario data.

tasks.title: Build an IP set and check the capacity of a rule
tasks.kills: "A network ACL is the place to block a long list of attacking IP addresses."
tasks.plan: AWS CloudShell, scope REGIONAL, one resource, no web ACL. 1) aws wafv2 create-ip-set: name saa-edge-protection-t01, IP version IPV4, addresses 192.0.2.0/24 (a documentation range), tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=edge-protection-t01; capture IPSET_ID (Summary.Id), IPSET_ARN (Summary.ARN). 2) aws wafv2 get-ip-set; capture LOCK_TOKEN (LockToken). 3) aws wafv2 check-capacity with inline rules: one IP set reference statement to $IPSET_ARN with action Block, and one rate-based statement with aggregate key IP and action Count; read the WCUs (compare with [1,500 WCUs] included, waf-wcu-included-1500, and [5,000 WCUs] at most, waf-max-wcu-per-web-acl). 4) Break it: predict 'Will AWS WAF accept 0.0.0.0/0 in the set?', run update-ip-set with 0.0.0.0/0 and $LOCK_TOKEN, expect an invalid parameter error; explain: AWS WAF [supports all IPv4 and IPv6 CIDR ranges except for /0] (waf-ip-set-cidr-ipv4-ipv6-not-slash-0; the display holds backticks around /0: copy it exactly or request a display without them). 5) Fix: none needed; get-ip-set shows the set unchanged. Cleanup: get-ip-set for a fresh lock token if needed, then aws wafv2 delete-ip-set with $IPSET_ID and the lock token. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources with --tag-filters Key=task,Values=edge-protection-t01 returns nothing, pending fr-0039 (no fact yet that the Tagging API lists AWS WAF IP sets; park the verify until it is filled). Cost: $0: no web ACL is created, and AWS WAF charges for web ACLs, rules per web ACL and requests (waf-pricing-dimensions). Read-only alternative: aws wafv2 list-ip-sets --scope REGIONAL and aws wafv2 check-capacity only. Commands must come from the AWS WAF CLI reference or an official example page in the corpus.

tasks.title: Create a domain allow list for outbound traffic

tasks.plan: AWS CloudShell, one resource, no firewall. 1) aws network-firewall create-rule-group: name saa-edge-protection-t02, type STATEFUL, a small capacity, an inline rule group with RulesSourceList targets for one approved domain (for example .amazonaws.com), target types TLS_SNI and HTTP_HOST, generated rules type ALLOWLIST; tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=edge-protection-t02. 2) aws network-firewall describe-rule-group and read the generated rules: the list matches names in the SNI and the Host header (network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header). Optional third step instead of a break-it (medium: no break-it required). Cleanup: aws network-firewall delete-rule-group with the name and type. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources with --tag-filters Key=task,Values=edge-protection-t02 returns nothing, pending fr-0040. Cost: $0: no firewall is created, and Network Firewall pricing is based on the number of firewalls deployed and the traffic inspected (network-firewall-faq-pricing-dimensions). Write this task only if the tasks writer has time after edge-protection-t01; if it is not written, subsection 5 has no Try it callout.

speak.prompt: The attack came from 1,400 addresses. Why can we not block those addresses?
speak.note: The prompt is Ana's question of STARTUP.md word for word; if the speak lint refuses digits in the prompt, write 'fourteen hundred addresses' and report it. Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'web ACL' as 'a set of rules at our front end that reads every request' the first time. Short answer: we can block a list, but a rule that watches how fast each address signs in, plus a check for stolen passwords, keeps working when the addresses change. How: AWS WAF counts sign-in requests from each address and blocks the ones over the limit; the account takeover rule group checks sign-ins against stolen passwords. Watch: a limit per address also hits many real users who share one office address, so the limit needs tuning. In your case: 'How many of the bank's supervisors sign in from one office address?' Must not say: 'a network ACL can hold all of those addresses' (correct: twenty rules per network ACL by default, spoken form of vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl); 'the rule blocks every attacker exactly at the limit' (correct: it counts each address separately; waf-rate-based-counts-and-limits). Numbers in the script as words, copied from the fact cards.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Do I need Shield Advanced, or are AWS WAF and Shield Standard enough?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: for most startups, Shield Standard plus AWS WAF is enough; Shield Advanced is for when downtime or an attack bill would hurt more than the fee. How: Shield Standard is automatic and free at layers three and four; AWS WAF rules stop web floods and exploits; Shield Advanced adds the response team at any hour and credits for scaling charges. Watch: Shield Advanced costs three thousand dollars per month (spoken form from the fact card) with a one-year subscription commitment. In your case: 'What would one hour of downtime cost you, and which support plan do you have?' Must not say: 'Shield Standard works only after you turn it on' (correct: automatic, at no additional charge); 'Shield Advanced protects all your resources automatically' (correct: only the resources you specify; shield-advanced-not-automatic-per-resource is a fact you may add to facts).

diagrams.title: Where each protection checks the traffic
diagrams.claim: Shield guards the edge, AWS WAF checks each web request, and Network Firewall checks traffic that leaves the VPC.
diagrams.alt: A path from users to an application. Users reach CloudFront at an edge location, guarded by Shield Standard. A web ACL of AWS WAF checks each request. The load balancer and the application sit in a VPC. Outbound traffic passes a Network Firewall endpoint.
say: A request from the internet reaches CloudFront at an edge location, where Shield Standard protects against network and transport layer DDoS attacks.
CloudFront sends the request to AWS WAF, and the web ACL allows or blocks it.
An allowed request goes on to the Application Load Balancer and the application in the VPC.
A request from the application to the internet passes a Network Firewall endpoint before the NAT gateway.
diagrams.note: Step 1 holds the display 'network and transport layer DDoS attacks' of shield-standard-automatic-no-charge: link it in the Markdown step. One Availability Zone is enough; no AWS number in labels. Hero kind arch, size s.

diagrams.placement: 2-deep.md#how-it-works (intro, before the first H3; fallback: end of subsection 6 before its Say it)
diagrams.title: Which service stops which threat
diagrams.claim: Ask where the threat travels, and the answer names the service that stops it.
diagrams.alt: A ladder of four questions. A flood of packets: AWS Shield. Harmful content or too many requests in web traffic: AWS WAF. Traffic that enters or leaves a VPC and needs domain or protocol rules: AWS Network Firewall. The same rules in every account: AWS Firewall Manager.
rungs: Is it a flood of packets? -> AWS Shield
Is it inside web requests? -> AWS WAF
Does it enter or leave a VPC? -> AWS Network Firewall
Must every account get the rules? -> AWS Firewall Manager
diagrams.note: Ladder: at most 6 rungs, questions of at most 9 words, one outcome per rung. The caption has no absolute word and no number, so it needs no link.

diagrams.title: Callvale before: the sign-in flood reaches the application
diagrams.claim: Without a web ACL, the sign-in flood passes CloudFront and the load balancer and reaches the application.
diagrams.alt: Before: attackers send sign-in requests to CloudFront, then to the Application Load Balancer and the application in private subnets. The application reaches any internet domain through NAT gateways.
say: Automated sign-in requests from many IP addresses reach CloudFront.
CloudFront and the Application Load Balancer pass each request on, because no web ACL checks it.
Workloads in the private subnets reach any domain on the internet through the NAT gateways.
diagrams.note: Story picture; the steps state no AWS rule. Keep each component in the same grid cell as in edge-protection-after (users left, CloudFront, load balancer, application, NAT gateway, internet right). Draw one Availability Zone; label 'NAT gateway in each Availability Zone' as story. No story numbers in labels except none needed.

diagrams.title: Callvale after: web ACLs at the edge and Network Firewall for outbound traffic
diagrams.claim: Web ACLs on CloudFront and the load balancer stop the flood, and outbound traffic passes Network Firewall to approved domains.
diagrams.alt: After: a web ACL on CloudFront blocks the flood, and the load balancer has its own web ACL. Firewall Manager applies one policy to all accounts. Outbound traffic passes a Network Firewall endpoint to approved domains, then the NAT gateway.
say: The web ACL on CloudFront blocks addresses that send too many sign-in requests and requests that match common attacks.
Requests that pass go to the Application Load Balancer, which has its own web ACL from the same Firewall Manager policy.
Outbound traffic from the private subnets goes to a Network Firewall endpoint in its own zone, which passes approved domains to the NAT gateway.
diagrams.note: Firewall Manager is a node in 'an administrator account' with labelled (not numbered) edges 'applies policy' to both web ACLs. At most 12 nodes. No Shield Advanced node (not bought). The steps avoid absolute words, so no link is required; link a fact if a step states one.
